rounds.text: Coromandel Engineering Company Ltd is currently undergoing a dramatic operational turnaround that the market has yet to fully price in. While historical growth metrics have been negative [E14, E15, E16], the company has achieved a 54% compounded sales growth over the trailing twelve months [E17]. This pivot is supported by an exceptional Return on Assets of 12.07%, which dwarfs the sector benchmark of 1.49% [E8]. Such efficiency suggests that the company is generating significantly more value from its existing asset base than its peers [E8]. Conceded: the P/E and P/B ratios are currently elevated relative to sector benchmarks [E6, E7], and the dividend yield is 0.00% [E4]. However, the recent surge in sales growth indicates that the business is successfully transitioning from a period of contraction to one of rapid expansion [E17]. The current market capitalisation of ₹ 187 Cr leaves substantial room for re-rating as this fundamental momentum continues to manifest [E3, E52].

Coromandel Engineering Company Ltd currently trades at a P/E ratio of 153x [E1] and a P/B ratio of 13.71x [E2], metrics that appear significantly detached from reality when compared to sector benchmarks of 26.6x and 1.5x respectively [E6, E7]. This extreme valuation is particularly concerning given the company’s long-term trajectory, which includes compounded sales growth of -10% over ten years, -17% over five years, and -30% over three years [E14, E15, E16]. The market’s current pricing reflects an aggressive optimism that is not supported by historical performance, as evidenced by the fact that price growth has outpaced profit growth by 32% [E52]. Furthermore, the stock offers no dividend yield to compensate investors for these risks [E4] and currently sits at the bottom of its 52-week range [E5]. Conceded: the company has achieved an ROA of 12.07% against a sector benchmark of 1.49% [E8] and a recent TTM sales growth of 54% [E17]. Despite these isolated positive indicators, the persistent multi-year decline in sales [E58] suggests that the current valuation is fundamentally disconnected from the company’s actual output [E52].

The bear’s focus on historical sales decline [E14, E15, E16] ignores the critical inflection point evidenced by the 54% compounded sales growth over the trailing twelve months [E17]. While the bear highlights high valuation multiples [E1, E2, E6, E7], these metrics fail to account for the company’s superior operational efficiency, as demonstrated by an ROA of 12.07% compared to the sector benchmark of 1.49% [E8]. Conceded: the company has a 0.00% dividend yield [E4] and has experienced long-term negative sales growth [E58]. The bear interprets the 32% gap between price and profit growth as a disconnect [E52], but this is more accurately viewed as the market pricing in the rapid turnaround in sales momentum [E17]. By trading near the bottom of its 52-week range [E5], the stock offers an entry point that reflects the historical baggage rather than the current, high-growth reality [E17]. Ultimately, the bear’s reliance on multi-year averages [E14, E15, E16] obscures the significant operational improvement and asset utilization [E8] that define the company's current trajectory.

The bull’s reliance on a single year of growth [E17] ignores the structural decay evidenced by the 10-year, 5-year, and 3-year compounded sales growth figures of -10%, -17%, and -30% respectively [E14, E15, E16]. While the bull cites superior ROA [E8], this efficiency metric cannot justify a P/E ratio of 1072.6x against a sector benchmark of 26.6x [E6] or a P/B of 17.1x against a sector benchmark of 1.5x [E7]. Conceded: the company has achieved a 54% growth rate in the trailing twelve months [E17] and an ROA of 12.07% [E8]. However, the market’s aggressive pricing is disconnected from reality, as evidenced by the fact that price growth currently exceeds profit growth by 32% [E52]. The stock’s position at only 7% of its 52-week range [E5] suggests that the market has already begun to discount the sustainability of the recent turnaround, rather than viewing it as a long-term growth trajectory. Relying on a short-term spike to justify extreme valuation multiples [E1, E2] is speculative when measured against the persistent, multi-year trend of declining sales [E58].
